title: Which circle goes with each fractional unit?
description: Four circles each have one shaded part, and four fractional units are to be matched with them. The equal parts in each circle are counted, and each unit is matched by its bottom number.
teaching_notes: One idea: one shaded part of a circle cut into equal parts is one over the number of equal parts. Watch for students who match the biggest bottom number with the biggest shaded part.

source: Match each fractional unit with the correct picture: 1/3, 1/5, 1/8, 1/6.
video_script.why: The child counts the equal parts in each circle and matches each fractional unit by the number of equal parts in the circle.
video_script.substitution: Treat each circle as a roti cut into equal parts, and count the parts the way the strip parts were counted.
video_script.anchor: Four circles, each cut into equal parts with one part shaded, beside the units one third, one fifth, one eighth and one sixth
video_script.payoff_line: Each unit matches the circle with that many equal parts

final_answer.value: 1/3 matches the circle with 3 parts, 1/5 matches the circle with 5 parts, 1/8 matches the circle with 8 parts, 1/6 matches the circle with 6 parts
final_answer.spoken: one third matches the circle of three parts, one fifth the circle of five parts, one eighth the circle of eight parts, and one sixth the circle of six parts

video_script.fraction_reading: one third, one fifth, one eighth, one sixth
never_show: any match between a unit and a circle before the answer beat
maths_rules: the four circles have 8, 6, 3 and 5 equal parts, with one part shaded in each
one shaded part of n equal parts is 1/n
1/3 matches the circle with 3 parts; 1/5 matches 5 parts; 1/8 matches 8 parts; 1/6 matches 6 parts
check: the bottom number of each unit equals the number of equal parts in its circle
video_script.design: One idea: count the equal parts, because that count is the bottom number. Same method as naming a strip part. The four circles and the four units stay on the board to the end.
open_questions: The book text has no description of the four circles; the part counts 8, 6, 3 and 5 come from the worklist and could not be checked against the figure.
